prompt: Which of these does a browser do?
optionA: Stores every page on the web for offline use
optionB: Requests files and turns them into what appears on screen
optionC: Runs the server that holds the pages
optionD: Provides the connection between machines
correctAnswerText: Requests files and turns them into what appears on screen
explanation: A browser asks for files and renders them. It holds only what it has recently fetched, the server runs elsewhere, and the network is what carries the request.

prompt: Is a browser the same thing as the internet?
optionA: Yes; the browser is how the internet is delivered
optionB: Yes; without a browser there is no internet
optionC: No; a browser is the internet plus the operating system
optionD: No; a browser is one program for using the web, which is carried over the internet
correctAnswerText: No; a browser is one program for using the web, which is carried over the internet
explanation: The internet connects machines and carries many services; a browser is a program that uses one of them. Email and file transfer travel over the same internet without a browser.

prompt: A page appears on screen. Which part did the browser do?
optionA: Fetched the files and drew the result
optionB: Wrote the page's content
optionC: Decided what the page should say
optionD: Stored the page permanently on the machine
correctAnswerText: Fetched the files and drew the result
explanation: The browser obtains and renders; the content was authored elsewhere and lives on a server. Anything kept locally is a temporary copy rather than the page itself.

prompt: Two different browsers open the same address and show slightly different results. How is that possible?
optionA: The server sent different pages to each
optionB: One of the two browsers is faulty
optionC: Each browser renders the same files, and they may render some things differently
optionD: The address means something different in each browser
correctAnswerText: Each browser renders the same files, and they may render some things differently
explanation: Rendering is the browser's own work, so two of them can turn identical files into slightly different pictures. Nothing about the address or the server changes between them.

prompt: A browser is closed and reopened, and a page that was open loads again. Where did the page come from?
optionA: From the browser's memory, which survives being closed
optionB: From the server, or from a stored copy the browser kept — not from the browser's memory of it
optionC: From the operating system, which held the page
optionD: From the page itself, which reloads automatically
correctAnswerText: From the server, or from a stored copy the browser kept — not from the browser's memory of it
explanation: Closing a browser ends what it was holding in memory, so the page has to be obtained again. Whether that means contacting the server depends on what was cached.

prompt: In the address https://shop.example.com/orders/42, which part is the host?
optionA: https
optionB: /orders/42
optionC: https://shop.example.com
optionD: shop.example.com
correctAnswerText: shop.example.com
explanation: The host names the machine to contact and stops before the first slash of the path. The scheme at the front says how to talk to it and is not part of its name.

prompt: In the same address, which part is the path?
optionA: /orders/42
optionB: shop.example.com
optionC: https
optionD: shop.example.com/orders
correctAnswerText: /orders/42
explanation: The path is what follows the host and names what is wanted from it. Including part of the host confuses which machine to ask with what to ask it for.

prompt: In the address https://docs.example.com/guide, what is docs?
optionA: The first segment of the path
optionB: The name of the file being requested
optionC: Part of the host name
optionD: A parameter passed to the server
correctAnswerText: Part of the host name
explanation: Anything before the first single slash after the scheme belongs to the host, so docs is part of the machine's name. Reading it as a path segment would send the request to a different machine entirely.

prompt: What is a web address, in essence?
optionA: A type of memory used by the browser
optionB: An address identifying a resource and saying where to ask for it
optionC: A loop that fetches a page repeatedly
optionD: A part of the processor
correctAnswerText: An address identifying a resource and saying where to ask for it
explanation: An address names what is wanted and the machine that has it, which is what lets a browser make a request at all.

prompt: Which question can a browser's developer tools answer?
optionA: What code the server runs to produce the page
optionB: What other users are seeing right now
optionC: What the page will look like tomorrow
optionD: Which files this page requested and whether each one arrived
correctAnswerText: Which files this page requested and whether each one arrived
explanation: The tools show what this browser did and what it currently holds. Nothing about the server's own code is visible, because none of it is sent.

prompt: A change is made to a page using the browser's developer tools, and the page is reloaded. What happens to the change?
optionA: It is gone; the tools change the loaded page and not the file
optionB: It is saved to the file and persists
optionC: It is sent to the server and applied for everyone
optionD: It persists until the browser is closed
correctAnswerText: It is gone; the tools change the loaded page and not the file
explanation: The tools operate on what the browser is currently holding, which is rebuilt from the file on every load. Expecting an edit there to persist is the commonest first surprise.

prompt: Are developer tools a separate program from the browser?
optionA: Yes; they must be installed separately
optionB: Yes; they run on the server
optionC: No; they are part of the browser and show what it is doing
optionD: No; they are part of the operating system
correctAnswerText: No; they are part of the browser and show what it is doing
explanation: The tools are built into the browser, which is why they can see the requests it made and the page it built. A separate program would have no access to either.

prompt: A page looks wrong and the developer tools show the page structure containing exactly what was expected. What does that suggest?
optionA: The tools are showing a cached version
optionB: The structure is right, so the problem lies in how it is being presented or in the data shown
optionC: The server sent the wrong page
optionD: Nothing; the tools cannot show the structure
correctAnswerText: The structure is right, so the problem lies in how it is being presented or in the data shown
explanation: The tools show the live state, so a correct structure narrows the problem to presentation or content rather than to what was built. That is a real elimination rather than a dead end.

prompt: Put the stages of loading a page in order.
optionA: All the files arrive together, and the browser reads them
optionB: The images arrive, then the document that names them
optionC: The browser requests every file it might need, then reads the document
optionD: The document arrives, the browser reads it, and it requests the files the document names
correctAnswerText: The document arrives, the browser reads it, and it requests the files the document names
explanation: The browser cannot know which images and styles a page uses until it has read the document naming them. That is why the document arrives first and everything else follows.

prompt: A page appears with its text visible and its images still arriving. Is that a fault?
optionA: No; the browser renders what it has and fills in the rest as it arrives
optionB: Yes; a page should appear only once everything has arrived
optionC: Yes; the images should have arrived before the text
optionD: No; but only because the images are optional
correctAnswerText: No; the browser renders what it has and fills in the rest as it arrives
explanation: Rendering progressively is what makes a page usable before it is complete. Waiting for everything would leave a blank screen for as long as the slowest file took.

prompt: A page shows a message that appears nowhere in the file the server sent. How is that possible?
optionA: The server sent a different file from the one on disk
optionB: The browser invented the message
optionC: Something running in the page added it after loading
optionD: The file must contain it and the search was wrong
correctAnswerText: Something running in the page added it after loading
explanation: What arrives is a starting point, and code running in the page can change it afterwards. The live page and the file it came from are two different things.

prompt: A developer changes the live page using the tools and the file on the server is unchanged. Which view shows the change, and which does not?
optionA: Both show it, since they describe the same page
optionB: The live view shows it; viewing the file the server sent does not
optionC: Neither shows it, since the change was temporary
optionD: The file shows it; the live view reverts
correctAnswerText: The live view shows it; viewing the file the server sent does not
explanation: One view is the document as delivered and the other is what the browser currently holds. They agree until something modifies the page, and after that they are separate records.

prompt: A styling file is changed on the server. A returning visitor sees the old styling. Why?
optionA: The server did not save the change
optionB: The visitor is looking at a different site
optionC: The browser cannot display new styling until it restarts
optionD: The browser reused a stored copy of the file rather than fetching it again
correctAnswerText: The browser reused a stored copy of the file rather than fetching it again
explanation: A stored copy is used in place of a request, so the change on the server is never seen. The server has the new file and nobody asked it for one.

prompt: A page updates correctly but its styling does not. Both were changed on the server. What does that suggest about caching?
optionA: It applies to individual files, so one may be reused while another is fetched afresh
optionB: Caching applies to whole pages, so the whole page must be stale
optionC: The styling file was not changed after all
optionD: Caching cannot affect styling files
correctAnswerText: It applies to individual files, so one may be reused while another is fetched afresh
explanation: Each file is stored and reused on its own terms, which is why a page can be part fresh and part stale. Treating the page as a single unit cannot explain the mixture.

prompt: Some visitors see a change and others do not, and the file on the server is definitely the new one. Everyone is visiting the same address. What explains the split?
optionA: The server is sending different files to different visitors
optionB: The change was applied to only some of the servers
optionC: Those who have visited before are reusing a stored copy; new visitors have nothing stored
optionD: The visitors who see the change are using a different address
correctAnswerText: Those who have visited before are reusing a stored copy; new visitors have nothing stored
explanation: A split between returning and new visitors is exactly what a stored copy produces, since only returning visitors have one. The stem rules out the address and the file as differences.

prompt: A site stores a small piece of data in the browser. What happens to it on the next request to that site?
optionA: It stays in the browser and is never sent
optionB: It is sent along with the request
optionC: It is sent to every site the browser visits
optionD: It is deleted when the page closes
correctAnswerText: It is sent along with the request
explanation: Data stored this way travels with requests to the site that set it, which is what lets the server recognise a returning visitor. Sending it everywhere would leak it to every site.

prompt: One site stores a value in the browser. Can an unrelated site read it?
optionA: Yes; anything in the browser is available to any page
optionB: Yes, but only if both sites are open at once
optionC: No; unless the two sites use the same browser
optionD: No; stored data belongs to the site that set it
correctAnswerText: No; stored data belongs to the site that set it
explanation: Storage is separated by site, so one site cannot read another's values. Sharing a browser is exactly the situation the separation exists for.

prompt: A user clears their browser data and finds they must log in again everywhere. Nothing about their accounts changed and the sites are working normally. Why?
optionA: The values proving they were logged in were stored in the browser and have been removed
optionB: The sites deleted their accounts
optionC: The accounts were stored in the browser and are gone
optionD: Clearing data changes the browser's identity
correctAnswerText: The values proving they were logged in were stored in the browser and have been removed
explanation: Being logged in is carried by something stored locally and sent with each request, so removing it removes the evidence. The accounts themselves live on the servers and are untouched.

prompt: A page on one site displays an image hosted on another. Is that permitted?
optionA: No; a page may only use files from its own site
optionB: Yes, but only if the two sites agree in advance
optionC: Yes; displaying a resource from another site is ordinary
optionD: No; unless the image is copied first
correctAnswerText: Yes; displaying a resource from another site is ordinary
explanation: Pages routinely load images, styles and fonts from elsewhere. What is restricted is reading the contents of a response from another site, which is a different thing.

prompt: A page on one site makes a request to another site and cannot read the response. Was the request sent?
optionA: No; the browser blocked the request before it left
optionB: Usually yes; the browser withheld the response rather than preventing the request
optionC: No; the other server refused it
optionD: Yes, and the response was read but discarded by the page
correctAnswerText: Usually yes; the browser withheld the response rather than preventing the request
explanation: The restriction is on what the page may see, applied by the browser after the response arrives. That is why a request can have real effects on the other server while the page learns nothing.

prompt: A developer says another site is blocking their requests. The other server's logs show the requests arriving and being answered normally. Who is doing the blocking?
optionA: The other server, which must be refusing them
optionB: The network, which is dropping the responses
optionC: Nobody; the requests must not be arriving
optionD: The browser, which is withholding the response from the page
correctAnswerText: The browser, which is withholding the response from the page
explanation: The other server answering rules it out as the blocker, and the requests arriving rules out the network. What remains is the browser applying its own restriction on what the page may read.

prompt: A site stores a preference in the browser. The user opens the same site in a different browser on the same machine. Is the preference there?
optionA: No; storage belongs to the browser that set it
optionB: Yes; it is stored on the machine
optionC: Yes; it follows the user
optionD: Only if both browsers are open at once
correctAnswerText: No; storage belongs to the browser that set it
explanation: Each browser keeps its own storage, so the same machine can hold several independent copies. Following the user would require an account rather than local storage.

prompt: The same user opens the site on their phone. Is the preference stored on their laptop available there?
optionA: Yes; preferences follow the user across devices
optionB: Yes, if both devices use the same browser brand
optionC: No; the two devices have separate storage and nothing synchronises it automatically
optionD: Only after the site is opened on both
correctAnswerText: No; the two devices have separate storage and nothing synchronises it automatically
explanation: Storage is local to a browser on a device, so nothing crosses between them by itself. Anything that does follow a user has been sent to a server and associated with an account.

prompt: A site keeps a user's settings and they survive closing the browser but vanish when the user switches machines. The user is signed in to the site on both machines. What does that tell you about where the settings are held?
optionA: On the server, associated with the account
optionB: In the browser rather than with the account, since signing in does not bring them across
optionC: In the operating system, which differs between machines
optionD: Nowhere; they are recreated each time
correctAnswerText: In the browser rather than with the account, since signing in does not bring them across
explanation: Surviving a restart rules out memory, and not following the signed-in account rules out the server. Local storage is exactly what persists on one machine and nowhere else.

prompt: A request list shows: page.html 200, style.css 404, logo.png 200. Which file failed?
optionA: page.html
optionB: logo.png
optionC: None of them
optionD: style.css
correctAnswerText: style.css
explanation: A status of 404 means the file was not found, and the other two succeeded. The page will render with its content and without its styling.

prompt: A request list shows: page.html 200 from the server, style.css 200 from cache, app.js 200 from the server. Which file did not reach the server on this load?
optionA: style.css
optionB: page.html
optionC: app.js
optionD: All three reached the server
correctAnswerText: style.css
explanation: A response served from cache never left the browser, so the server saw two requests rather than three. Reading a cached response as a fresh one is what hides a stale file.

prompt: A page renders unstyled. The request list shows page.html 200, style.css 404, and no other failures. The styling file exists on the server under a slightly different name. What is the cause?
optionA: The styling file is corrupt
optionB: The browser cached a failed response
optionC: The page is asking for a name that does not exist, so the address in the page is wrong
optionD: The server is refusing to serve styling files
correctAnswerText: The page is asking for a name that does not exist, so the address in the page is wrong
explanation: A 404 means the server was reached and had nothing at that name, and the stem confirms the file exists under another. That places the fault in what the page asked for rather than in the server or the file.

prompt: A developer edits a file, reloads, and sees no change. The request list shows the file served from cache. What is the cause?
optionA: The edit was never saved
optionB: A stored copy is being reused, so the edited file was never fetched
optionC: The wrong file was edited
optionD: The change is present but has no visible effect
correctAnswerText: A stored copy is being reused, so the edited file was never fetched
explanation: The evidence names the cause directly: the browser did not ask for the file. The other explanations are real and would not show a cached response.

prompt: A developer edits a file, reloads, and sees no change. The request list shows the file fetched fresh from the server with a 200 status. What are the remaining explanations?
optionA: A cached copy is being used
optionB: The server is down
optionC: The browser is displaying an old page from memory
optionD: The edit was not saved, or the file being served is not the one edited
correctAnswerText: The edit was not saved, or the file being served is not the one edited
explanation: A fresh fetch rules caching out, so the file the server sent did not contain the change. Either it was never written to disk or the server is serving a different copy — which is why "did you save it" and "which file is being served" are both worth asking.

prompt: A form checks in the browser that an age is at least 18 before submitting. Is that check enough on its own?
optionA: No; the check runs on the user's machine and can be bypassed
optionB: Yes; the form cannot be submitted otherwise
optionC: Yes, provided the check is written correctly
optionD: No; but only if the user knows how to use developer tools
correctAnswerText: No; the check runs on the user's machine and can be bypassed
explanation: Anything running in the browser is under the user's control, so the check improves the experience and enforces nothing. Whether a particular user knows how to bypass it does not change what the check guarantees.

prompt: A button that performs an administrative action is hidden from ordinary users by the page. The hiding works correctly and no ordinary user sees the button. Is the action protected?
optionA: Yes; the users cannot see it
optionB: Yes, provided the hiding cannot be undone
optionC: No; hiding a control does not prevent the request it would have made
optionD: No; the button should be removed rather than hidden
correctAnswerText: No; hiding a control does not prevent the request it would have made
explanation: The request the button would send can be made without the button, so the protection has to be on the server. Removing the button entirely changes nothing about that, which is why it is not the fix.

prompt: A page displays its text correctly with no styling at all. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The document did not arrive
optionB: The styling file did not arrive
optionC: The server is down
optionD: The images failed to load
correctAnswerText: The styling file did not arrive
explanation: Text appearing at all proves the document arrived and the server answered. A missing styling file removes the presentation and leaves the content, which is exactly the symptom.

prompt: A page shows a broken image and everything else is correct. The request for that image returned a 404 and every other request succeeded. What follows?
optionA: The whole page failed to load
optionB: The image file is corrupt
optionC: The image was cached in a broken state
optionD: The image is not at the address the page asked for
correctAnswerText: The image is not at the address the page asked for
explanation: A single 404 among successes localises the fault to one file and to its address. A corrupt file would have been found and returned with a success status.

prompt: A page appears completely unstyled. Two files failed: the styling file and a font it references. How many causes need to be found?
optionA: Possibly one; if the styling file is missing, the font it references is never requested successfully either
optionB: Two, one for each failure
optionC: Two, since a font and a stylesheet are unrelated
optionD: None; the page is working as intended
correctAnswerText: Possibly one; if the styling file is missing, the font it references is never requested successfully either
explanation: Failures can be dependent, and one missing file can produce several entries in the list. Treating each as a separate cause means investigating something that will disappear on its own.

prompt: A page loads perfectly on the developer's machine and is unstyled for everyone else. The styling file is referenced by a path that works locally. What is the likely difference?
optionA: The other users have a caching problem
optionB: The server is refusing requests from other users
optionC: The path resolves to a file that exists only on the developer's machine
optionD: The styling file is too large for other connections
correctAnswerText: The path resolves to a file that exists only on the developer's machine
explanation: Something working in exactly one place points at what is present in that place and nowhere else. A cache would produce a stale page rather than an unstyled one for people who have never visited.

prompt: One symptom — a page without styling — has three candidate causes: the file is missing, the path is wrong, or a stale copy is cached. Which single piece of evidence separates them fastest?
optionA: Reloading the page repeatedly
optionB: The request list: a 404 means missing or misnamed, and a cached response means stale
optionC: Reading the styling file itself
optionD: Asking another user whether they see the same thing
correctAnswerText: The request list: a 404 means missing or misnamed, and a cached response means stale
explanation: The request list distinguishes all three at once, because each cause leaves a different entry in it. Asking another user is useful and answers a narrower question, and reading the file assumes the browser reached it.

prompt: A user browses in private mode so that others using the same laptop cannot see where they went. The mode works exactly as designed. Does it address their concern?
optionA: No; private mode keeps history like any other window
optionB: No; private mode only hides the browser window
optionC: Yes; and it also hides the visits from their network provider
optionD: Yes; local history and stored data are what private mode does not keep
correctAnswerText: Yes; local history and stored data are what private mode does not keep
explanation: The concern is about someone with access to the same machine, which is exactly what not retaining local records addresses. The last option is true of a different concern and is what makes the mode oversold.

prompt: A user browses in private mode so their employer's network cannot see which sites they visit. Does it address that?
optionA: No; the requests still travel over the same network and are as visible as ever
optionB: Yes; private mode encrypts all traffic
optionC: Yes; private mode routes traffic through another server
optionD: No; but only for sites that are not encrypted
correctAnswerText: No; the requests still travel over the same network and are as visible as ever
explanation: Private mode changes what the browser keeps locally and nothing about what leaves the machine. Encryption is a separate matter and hides the contents rather than which host was contacted.

prompt: A user browses in private mode so a site cannot recognise them as a returning visitor. Does it address that?
optionA: Yes, completely; the site sees a brand-new visitor
optionB: No; private mode has no effect on stored identifiers
optionC: Partly; stored identifiers are not carried over, and a site has other ways to recognise a returning visitor
optionD: Yes; private mode changes the address requests come from
correctAnswerText: Partly; stored identifiers are not carried over, and a site has other ways to recognise a returning visitor
explanation: Discarding stored values removes the most direct route to recognition and leaves others, so the honest answer is partial. Claiming complete anonymity is the belief this family exists to correct.

prompt: What is the single most accurate summary of what private browsing changes?
optionA: Who can see the traffic on the network
optionB: What the browser keeps on this machine after the window closes
optionC: Whether sites can identify the visitor
optionD: Whether the connection is encrypted
correctAnswerText: What the browser keeps on this machine after the window closes
explanation: Every capability of the mode follows from not retaining local records, and none of the other three follows from it at all. Holding the summary is what lets each specific concern be judged without memorising a list.

prompt: Private mode is often described as "browsing anonymously". What does that description cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is a fair short description
optionB: It understates what the mode does
optionC: It costs only accuracy, with no practical effect
optionD: It leads users to rely on it for concerns it does not address, such as network visibility
correctAnswerText: It leads users to rely on it for concerns it does not address, such as network visibility
explanation: A description that overstates a protection is worse than none, because someone will act on it. What is lost is not precision for its own sake but the user's ability to judge when the mode is enough.

prompt: A logo file has not changed in three years and is loaded on every page. What caching approach fits, and what does it cost?
optionA: Reuse it for a long time; the cost is that a change would take that long to reach returning visitors
optionB: Never reuse it, so it is always current
optionC: Reuse it for a few seconds, as a compromise
optionD: Reuse it forever, with no cost at all
correctAnswerText: Reuse it for a long time; the cost is that a change would take that long to reach returning visitors
explanation: Content that almost never changes is what long reuse is for, and the price is paid only when it does change. Claiming no cost ignores that a change becomes invisible for the reuse period.

prompt: A page shows a live share price that changes every few seconds. What caching approach fits?
optionA: Reuse for a few minutes, to reduce load
optionB: Reuse for a day, since the page structure is stable
optionC: None; the value must be fetched each time it is shown
optionD: Reuse forever, with a manual refresh available
correctAnswerText: None; the value must be fetched each time it is shown
explanation: Reuse is only acceptable while the stored copy is still true, and here that is a matter of seconds. The page structure may well be cached, and the value inside it cannot be.

prompt: A styling file changes about once a month, unpredictably. Long reuse makes pages fast and delays updates. How can both be had?
optionA: Reuse for exactly one month
optionB: Give the file a new name when it changes, so a long reuse period never delays an update
optionC: Never reuse it, and accept slower pages
optionD: Reuse it and ask users to clear their cache after each change
correctAnswerText: Give the file a new name when it changes, so a long reuse period never delays an update
explanation: Renaming makes the address change with the content, so a new file is fetched immediately while old ones stay reusable indefinitely. A fixed period is a guess about when the next change falls, and asking users to intervene puts the cost on them.

prompt: A team sets a short reuse period for everything, so nothing is ever stale. What does that choice cost?
optionA: Nothing; freshness is always worth having
optionB: Only server cost, since users notice nothing
optionC: Only user-visible speed, since servers are unaffected
optionD: Almost every visit re-fetches files that had not changed, which is slower for users and heavier for the server
correctAnswerText: Almost every visit re-fetches files that had not changed, which is slower for users and heavier for the server
explanation: A uniform short period treats content that never changes exactly like content that changes constantly, and pays the fetch cost on both. The cost lands on the user and the server together rather than on either alone.
